# Rounding in analysis and reporting {#sec-workflow-rounding}

::: callout-tip
An AI-first workflow can turn written business rules into continuous,
evidence-backed checks while keeping exceptions and policy decisions with
people.
:::

Imagine a Biometrics team preparing an adverse-event table. The display
specification calls for one decimal place and includes terms whose percentage
meets a reporting threshold. A reviewer notices that 2.5 percent becomes 3
following team convention but 2 in R's default `round()` function. This halfway
case is called a decimal tie. The difference can change both a displayed
statistic and whether a row passes the reporting threshold.

Common programming languages differ in their default handling of decimal ties:

| Language or tool | Default tie behavior | `-2.5` | `2.5` |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| SAS `ROUND()` | half away from zero | -3 | 3 |
| R `round()` | half to even | -2 | 2 |
| Python `round()` | half to even | -2 | 2 |

The lesson is not that one language is correct. A language default is an
implementation choice, not organizational policy. The convention is the policy,
and no line of source code states it.

This chapter stays at that level. It describes the problem, writes the rule
down, and sends one prompt to an agent to check a real R package against it.
The prompt produces a real finding. It does not produce a workflow.
@sec-workflow-rounding-skill takes the limits identified here and designs one.

The chapter has one main finding: **a prompt can find the problem but cannot
own it.**

- **Problem:** Rounding rules are applied inconsistently across programs,
  languages, and studies, and the rule is often unwritten.
- **Learning objective:** Show what a written business rule and a single
  well-specified prompt can accomplish, and what they leave undone.
- **Not in this chapter:** A task contract, a prototype, a benchmark, a release
  record, or any claim that the check is repeatable. Those belong to
  @sec-workflow-rounding-skill.

## Write the rule down before asking anyone to check it

A reviewer cannot ask an agent, a contractor, or a new team member to verify a
convention that exists only in habit. The first work is not a prompt. It is a
short, versioned statement of what the organization requires.

### Business rule: BR-NUM-001

BR-NUM-001 is an illustrative contract written for this book. It is not an
approved industry standard, and it is not the stated rule of any package
reviewed here. Version 1.0 contains three rules:

> **BR-NUM-001.1:** Values intended as exact decimal ties are rounded half away
> from zero. A displayed value is never a negative zero.

> **BR-NUM-001.2:** Calculations use unrounded values; rounding occurs once,
> when the final result is prepared for display.

> **BR-NUM-001.3:** Display precision is specified for each reported statistic
> and preserved, including trailing zeros.

Rule 3 covers a problem that is easy to overlook because it is not arithmetic.
The values `76`, `76.0`, and `76.00` are numerically equal, but they communicate
different precision in a table. A program can calculate the intended number and
still produce an output that violates a reporting convention.

### Define what counts as a rounding site

Writing the rule is not enough. The rule must also say where it applies. A
request to check that source code "properly rounds half away from zero" does not
say which calls count, and the answer changes completely depending on the
definition. BR-NUM-001 therefore carries a scope clause:

> A rounding site is any call that can change a numeric value displayed in a
> report or used to decide which rows the report includes. Formatting functions
> round as a side effect of display, so `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, and `format()`
> are candidate rounding sites. Finding one `round()` call does not establish
> complete coverage.

That clause is the difference between a review that inspects one function name
and a review that inspects the calls that actually reach the table. The rest of
this chapter shows how much difference it makes.

## The request a reviewer actually writes

A reviewer asked to check a package against BR-NUM-001 might begin with this:

> At `metalite.ae` version 0.1.4,
> verify whether the R source uses round half away from zero for reported
> values and report-filtering decisions. If not, identify the source and draft
> a GitHub issue to report the finding.

The request names a target and a rule, which is more than many review requests
do. It still does not say what counts as a rounding site, which files are in
scope, what test would demonstrate a violation, or who decides whether a
difference is a defect rather than an accepted local convention.

The review target is
[`Merck/metalite.ae` at a released version](https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/releases/tag/v0.1.4),
a public R package that analyzes adverse events from ADaM data and produces
tables, listings, and figures using the `metalite` data structure. The commit is
pinned because the package is maintained: an unpinned reference can silently
stop reproducing.

### Try it yourself

Send the following prompt to [arena.ai](https://arena.ai/agent) before reading
the rest of this chapter. It is the same request, rewritten to carry the scope
clause, the required evidence, and an explicit stop point.

```text
Review the R source of the metalite.ae package at the commit linked below.
Verify whether it follows this business rule: values intended as exact decimal
ties must round half away from zero.

Repository at fixed commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite.ae/tree/bdb23d472b16bc9dadbc774e64c5ca40321e9c6b

Do not propose a code change. Do not modify any repository. State what was and
was not checked.
```

Arena.ai cannot create the GitHub issue, so a draft is the expected endpoint.
Agent responses vary between runs, and that variability is part of the lesson.
Do not treat any particular response as the answer key. Judge the response you
receive by asking:

- Did it inspect formatting functions as well as `round()`?
- Did it give locations at the pinned commit rather than general advice?
- Did it demonstrate behavior at ties of both signs?
- Did it state what it checked and what it did not?

## What the scope clause changes

At the pinned commit, a search of the R source for `round(` returns one match.
Read without the scope clause, that looks close to a clean result.

It is not. The single `round()` call is a report decision: a rounded percentage
controls whether an adverse-event row passes the reporting threshold. A review
that applies the scope clause finds seven more sites, all in display helpers,
that round percentages, estimates, standard deviations, confidence-interval
limits, p-values, and exposure-adjusted event rates before they reach the table.

| What the reviewer searches for | Sites found at the pinned commit |
|---|---|
| Calls named `round(` | 1 report-filtering decision |
| Every call meeting the scope clause | 1 report-filtering decision and 7 display sites |

The eight sites, their file and line numbers, the decimal-tie evidence for each,
and the reason the display helpers diverge are recorded in
@sec-workflow-rounding-skill, where they serve as the benchmark answer key. The
point here is narrower: the prompt did not determine the result. The definition
of a rounding site did.

## What one prompt cannot give you

The prompt produced a genuine finding, and a Biometrics team could act on it.
Four things are still missing, and none of them can be fixed by rewording the
prompt.

- **Coverage.** The response describes what it found. It does not establish
  which files were examined, which were skipped, or which of the three rules
  went unchecked. Silence is not evidence that everything was reviewed.
- **Repeatability.** The result depends on one carefully written prompt held by
  one reviewer. A colleague repeating the review next quarter reconstructs the
  scope clause, the tie values, and the stop point from memory, or does not
  reconstruct them at all.
- **Separation of fixed checks from judgment.** Locating candidate calls and
  probing them at decimal ties are mechanical steps that should give the same
  answer every time. Deciding whether a candidate reaches the report is
  judgment. A single response blends them, so a reader cannot tell which claims
  are reproducible.
- **A named human gate.** Nothing in the exchange records who classifies each
  finding as a defect, a documented convention, an accepted exception, or not
  applicable, or who authorizes telling anyone outside the team.

These four gaps are the requirements for the next chapter. They are also the
reason the drafted GitHub issue stays a draft: `metalite.ae` is another team's
repository, it does not state BR-NUM-001 as its rule, and no accountable person
has classified the evidence as a defect.

## Summary

Rounding looks like a settled question until two tools disagree at a tie. The
disagreement is not a bug in a language; it is an unwritten policy. Writing
BR-NUM-001 down, and defining where it applies, is what made a check possible at
all, and the scope clause changed a one-site search into an eight-site finding.

A single prompt was enough to surface that finding. It was not enough to state
coverage, to run the same way twice, to keep deterministic results apart from
judgment, or to name who decides. @sec-workflow-rounding-skill designs a
workflow that does.
